questions.q: What does this lesson say happens when a project tries to treat every requirement as equally urgent?
options: The project ships faster than if requirements were prioritized
The project ends up deciding priority anyway, just badly and under pressure, often by whatever was discussed most recently or loudest
Nothing changes; prioritization has no real effect on outcomes
Every requirement automatically becomes a Must have by Salesforce's own rules
questions.explain: Having too many requirements for the available time and budget is normal. Refusing to deliberately prioritize doesn't avoid the decision — it just makes it badly, under pressure, usually driven by recency or volume rather than actual importance.

questions.q: In the MoSCoW method, what defines a "Must have" requirement?
options: Anything a senior stakeholder personally requested
Something the solution fails its core purpose without
The requirement that was identified first in the project
Any requirement that involves a new custom object
questions.explain: A Must have is defined by what happens without it: the solution doesn't actually meet its core purpose. That's a higher bar than "important" or "wanted" — those map to Should or Could.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the "Won't have (this time)" bucket, as opposed to simply not mentioning a requirement at all?
options: It signals the requirement is a bad idea that will never be built
It explicitly names a deferred requirement, preventing it from quietly resurfacing later as a surprise expectation
It means the requirement failed quality review
It is identical in meaning to "Could have"
questions.explain: Naming something "Won't have this time" out loud, rather than letting it silently drop off the list, prevents it from becoming an unpleasant surprise expectation when someone assumes it was included.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say prioritization isn't purely a product-owner decision?
options: Because product owners are not allowed to make prioritization decisions under Salesforce governance rules
Because an architect can surface technical information, like shared dependencies between requirements, that the business side may not see on its own
Because architects always outrank product owners in a project
Because prioritization is purely a random process with no real inputs
questions.explain: A requirement that looks independent or low-priority in isolation might actually be nearly free to deliver alongside a Must have because they share underlying infrastructure — information an architect is positioned to surface that a purely business-side prioritization conversation might miss.

questions.q: What is the recommended response when a stakeholder labels every requirement "Must have"?
options: Immediately tell them they are wrong about all of their requirements
Accept all labels as given and build everything regardless of the deadline
Reframe the question by forcing a real trade-off, e.g. asking which three of ten Musts they'd pick if only three could ship by the deadline
Escalate the disagreement to a Salesforce support case
questions.explain: Rather than arguing about whether the requirements matter, forcing a concrete trade-off under a real constraint (a fixed deadline or budget) makes "everything is critical" collapse into an actual, honest ranking.
